saya.note: A polite, widely usable way to refer to yourself.
saya.example: Saya makan nasi. → I eat rice.

awak.note: Common in familiar conversation. With strangers or in formal settings, a name or title may be more appropriate.
awak.example: Awak minum air. → You drink water.

dia.note: The same pronoun refers to he or she. Malay does not mark gender here.
dia.example: Dia baca buku. → He / she reads a book.

kami.note: The speaker’s group, excluding the person being addressed.
kami.example: Kami makan nasi. → We eat rice (you are not included).

kita.note: The speaker’s group, including the person being addressed.
kita.example: Kita makan nasi. → We eat rice (you are included).

makan.note: This base form is widely used. Malay verbs do not change for I, you, or we.
makan.example: Saya makan. Dia makan. → I eat. He / she eats.

minum.note: A common base verb. The sentence context tells you when the drinking happens.
minum.example: Saya minum air. → I drink water.

baca.note: A root form often used in conversation. Membaca is the standard active form in formal writing.
baca.example: Dia baca buku. → He / she reads a book. (Conversational)

tulis.note: A root form often used in conversation. In the standard active form, meN- + tulis becomes menulis: the initial t drops.
tulis.example: Saya tulis surat. → I write a letter. (Conversational)

beli.note: A root form often used in conversation. Membeli is the standard active form in formal writing.
beli.example: Awak beli buku. → You buy a book. (Conversational)

nasi.note: Nasi means cooked rice. Malay often leaves articles such as a, an, and the implicit.
nasi.example: Saya makan nasi. → I eat rice.

air.note: In Malay, air means water. It is not the English word air.
air.example: Dia minum air. → He / she drinks water.

buku.note: A noun with no grammatical gender. A book or the book depends on context.
buku.example: Saya baca buku. → I read a book.

surat.note: Here, a written letter. The article a is supplied naturally in the English translation.
surat.example: Saya tulis surat. → I write a letter.

sedang.note: An aspect marker placed before the verb. It explicitly shows an action is ongoing.
sedang.example: Saya sedang makan. → I am eating.

membaca.note: meN- + baca → membaca. The prefix appears as mem- before b. It marks an active verb here, not tense or ongoing action.
membaca.example: Saya membaca buku. → I read a book.

menulis.note: meN- + tulis → menulis. The initial t drops in this standard form. The prefix does not mean continuous action.
menulis.example: Dia menulis surat. → He / she writes a letter.

membeli.note: meN- + beli → membeli. The prefix appears as mem- before b. This is the standard active form.
membeli.example: Kami membeli buku. → We buy a book.

roti.note: A new object in a familiar pattern. Keep the sentence structure; swap just one word.
roti.example: Saya makan roti. → I eat bread.

teh.note: Another object for minum. Malay does not require an article before it.
teh.example: Awak minum teh. → You drink tea.
